A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark and clinical unlearning experiments, ablations, timing measurements, and model-composition results.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and clinical results, ablations, hyperparameter analyses, and timing measurements, although the composition study is removed.

M1.justification: The boundary-search updates, relabeling, fine-tuning, and optional remain-loss and soft-logit procedures remain unchanged in Algorithms 1–3. Heuristic details move to Appendix A.5. Composition remains briefly mentioned; its experimental demonstration and detailed configurations are removed without introducing a replacement procedure.

E1.justification: The six main-text datasets, clinical device/anatomical scenarios, and appendix heatmaps labeled OCT and US are retained. Changing DRIONS-DB to IDRiD and correcting the MRI class count match information already present in v2's Table 3 and class list, rather than establishing new coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark and clinical comparisons retain Retrain, Finetune, NegGrad, CFK, EUK, Scrub, and Boundary. Removed related-work citations do not represent removed evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 Section 2.6 specifies 15 epochs for medical ResNet-50 fine-tuning, whereas v3 Section 3.2 states training until convergence. This revises the reported training budget and resolves mixed stopping descriptions in v2; it does not establish that experiments were rerun. Splits, metrics, and benchmark training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Section 3.4 and Figure 8 test whether combining complementary feature extractors and classifier heads, followed by fine-tuning, improves forgetting and retention. This entire composition study disappears. The loss/logit ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, clinical examples, and decision-boundary analyses remain; v3's expanded main ablation table already existed in v2's appendix.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-fold MIA cross-validation and the same mean-and-standard-deviation reporting practice. No new seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance procedures are reported. Highlighting MIA values closest to 0.5 changes presentation, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 removes the composition results, including Composition 2's F-Acc of 0 and R-Acc of 0.907 after one fine-tuning epoch, the epoch-wise curves, and composition-specific timing claims. Clinical Table 1, all 48 selective-unlearning result rows, and matched ablation tables retain their values. The substantial difference is withdrawn evidence, not a measured performance decline.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.6 supplies a probability/pigeonhole argument explaining that a true-class probability of 1/K places a point on or across a boundary, with exact pairwise-boundary correspondence in binary classification. This qualifies the earlier exact-projection description. The existing lemmas, convergence theorem, and proofs otherwise remain unchanged apart from numbering.

C1.justification: v3 removes the headline contribution that compositional reuse produces hybrid models outperforming their constituents and retraining. The introduction replaces 'exact' unlearning with sample-level terminology, and the abstract narrows the concluding emphasis from an established modular alternative to retraining to demonstrated clinical feasibility. Composition survives only as a brief heuristic mention.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly distinguishes enforced misclassification from retraining-based statistical indistinguishability and limits its privacy interpretation. The discussion adds possible explanations for elevated MIA scores, stronger hyperparameter-sensitivity qualifications, and acknowledgment that device removal has not demonstrated future-performance benefits. New Section 6 addresses patient misclassification, subgroup bias, and safeguards for clinical deployment.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link, explicitly states that medical images receive no additional unlearning-specific preprocessing, and discloses gamma = 0 for the ablations. Conversely, composition-specific module pairings, hyperparameter configurations, and fine-tuning timing details disappear. Core pseudocode, hardware information, and most training details are retained.

R1.justification: The shortened related-work discussion removes references including Chien's Langevin unlearning and the medical-unlearning works by Xue and Nasirigerdeh. Additions include domain-adaptation surveys, Nguyen's unlearning survey, and another Nahass work. Chen et al. remains the central predecessor, with its relationship to the proposed method clarified in Remark 2.6.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work narrative are substantially reorganized, experimental settings become a separate Experiments section, and detailed outer-loop heuristics move to the appendix. The composition section is removed, the discussion is extensively rewritten, and separate healthcare-implications and disclosure sections are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn into labeled stages. Clinical examples move from main-text Figure 3 to appendix Figure 6, the composition figure disappears, and v2's full appendix ablation table replaces its abbreviated main-table presentation. Percentage-axis labels and MIA highlighting are revised, alongside extensive publication-format changes to typography, tables, and page layout.

improvement.justification: v3 improves the interpretation of the retained evidence by explicitly separating behavioral suppression from standard privacy-oriented unlearning and addressing clinical deployment risks. The threshold qualification and code-access information also improve documentation. These gains are limited by the removal of composition evidence and implementation details while composition remains briefly advertised, leaving that extension less well supported.
